newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Tsar Peter the Great causes monumental Moscow row.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Tsar Peter the Great causes monumental Moscow row.

text.p: Three centuries after he forsook Moscow to build himself a new capital in St Petersburg, Peter the Great is back in the city he despised -- and may face expulsion.
Many Moscovites loathe a new 60-metre (196 feet) statue of the tsar which has arisen on the banks of the Moscow river, calling it an eyesore of colossal proportions.
"It is ugly, it is horrible," said Sergei, a 37-year-old engineer walking around the latest oevre of Moscow monumentalist sculptor Zurab Tsereteli.

The work shows the tsar, holding a ship's wheel as a symbol of the Russian fleet he created in the 18th century, on a huge spiked pedestal in the style of the bows of an ancient Roman warship. The monument looks something like a dragon's tail.
Tsereteli's homage to the tsar has triggered a wave of discontent among the population of Moscow, which is tired of massive artistic monuments of often dubious quality.
A group of protestors, led by Moscow gallery-owner Murat Gelman, is demanding its demolition and threatening to organise a costly city referendum on the future of the iron tsar.
"We do not think that a monument of such proportions should be placed in the city centre," Roman Tkash, one of the anti-Peter activists, told Reuters.

According to Moscow law, the city must hold a referendum if anybody gathers 100,000 signatures on a specific issue. Such a poll would cost several million dollars and burden the budget of the already cash-strapped capital.
President Boris Yeltsin has joined the protests, saying he has had enough of Tsereteli's controversial statues, which already adorn many parts of Moscow.

"I recently have more than once criticised Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov and sculptor Tsereteli, especially for the monument to Peter," Yeltsin said. "Moscow's backing of Tsereteli is a vain thing. Don't we have other sculptors and artists?"

Tsereteli, who likes his statues tall and pointed, became Russia's most controversial artist after Lushkov commissioned for a series of projects, including a centerpiece to a World War Two museum which opened in 1995.

The monument outside the museum is a tall obelisk adorned with cherubs and a goddess and embossed with the names of the Soviet Union's hero cities in the war against Nazi Germany. Irreverent critics have dubbed it the "monkey on a stick".
Luzhkov, an ambitious and popular politician who some say might become Yeltsin's successor, was miffed by the protests. And so was Tsereteli.
The Interfax news agency quoted Luzhkov as saying the protests amounted to "persecution".

"He expressed amazement that any ordinary journalist, even one who entered journalism straight from college, could judge culture with such frivolity," the agency quoted the mayor as saying in January.
Luzhkov then created a commisson to deal with the public pressure and said it would decide on Peter's future within weeks.
Not everyone who hates the monument is in favour of its demolition. "That will cost even more money," said Sergei.
Moscow officials say the cost of the monument, once finished, would be 100 billion roubles ($17.5 million), while it would cost 30 to 50 billion roubles to dismantle it.
